utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we've delayed you for a few minutes - I hope we haven't - it's due to slight problems with the first witness, K12. May he come into court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration. Yes. Just read out what's on the card, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are going to be known in these proceedings as Witness K12. The usher will show you a piece of paper which has on it a name, a date of birth, and the words "Pseudonym K12." Would you please look at the piece of paper, read it to yourself and simply say yes, the only word to be said, if the name and date of birth are yours. If they're not yours, say no, but if they are yours, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that piece of paper please be processed in the usual way. We have, I'm afraid, only a small map, the one with which you're familiar, showing all the areas referred to by this witness, but I think the areas in Serbia to which he needs refer at the moment will be sufficiently identified if identified by an area. May this bit, please, the very first bit -- may the first part of the testimony please be given in closed session, as it's conceivable that it would identify the witness. Or in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness K12, did you do Yugoslav army national service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: Yes, I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What years was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What job did you do in national service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: Driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have any basic military training as well as the necessary training to be a military driver? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following national service, did you return to civilian life and work as a truck driver for several years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have a woman with whom you shared your life - just yes or no - but to whom you were not in fact formally married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: I don't want to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In February 1999, did something happen when people came to your house? Just yes or no first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: Be reasonable. Don't confuse me here. Do you understand this language that I'm speaking? Do you understand what I mean when I say I can't?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd like you, please, to listen to the question. In February 1999, did men come to your house? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: Are they being obstinate or what? If I say I cannot cooperate in that sense, then I can't. Don't ask me 100 times. I tell you, I'm not going to lose my nerves here and keep drinking water and whatever. I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're here to tell the truth. You should bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the truth, the truth is that I cannot testify, and there is no other truth but that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. K12, could you kindly give me the reason to the Court why you can't give the -- your testimony again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should -- does this suit you: Do you want -- do you want me to give additional explanations and jeopardise other people in the process? Is this in line with your regulations? Tell me that first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have no idea what's happening to you or to your family. So could you kindly give me some rough information about that? Mr. K12, you gave witness statements to the Prosecution on all your days, and you were given this kind of protection in which your identity will not be open to the public, and there are lot more -- some protective measures taken. Can we take a look at the magazine? Could it be on the ELMO. No. Ah, yes. The Judges, the Chamber will take a look first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K12, we will hand your magazine back. Mr. Nice, I don't think at the moment it's worth taking this matter any further unless there are further questions you think it's worth asking. It doesn't sound like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. There's obviously an application I might in due course make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then there are considerations the Chamber might in due course itself have to give to a reluctant witness. I have to say that the -- today's attitude is not entirely unprecedented in a history that's been changeable. But if, notwithstanding the fact that he started to give evidence and bearing in mind that he hasn't given any evidence of substance, if we may have leave to speak to him, may his testimony be adjourned, and we will keep a note of what passes between us? Not necessarily on the basis that all of it will be available to the accused because there may be things said that won't be available, but we will keep a note of what passes and revert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But when -- how would that coincide with the application that you might make? There might be -- the one might not be consistent with the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, yes. I simply won't touch in those discussions on the application that I might make to the Chamber. I'll simply deal in these discussions, or Ms. Romano, will, if I am for the time being dealing with another witness, on willingness and on the other issues that I raised a few minutes ago but not on the application that I will be making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Witness K12, we're going to adjourn your evidence, which means this: That you're to speak to a member of the Prosecution. You are to review your position, your duty to tell the truth. Also, you should carefully consider your position generally. Very well. The matter is adjourned. You may leave now. Yes. Let the witness go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we come to the morning break, and they're typically 20 minutes, I might conceivably ask for just a few minutes more if I'm engaged in a discussion with the witness, but I'll try and keep it to 20 minutes. There may, of course, be nothing for me to say. Right. The next witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Awhile ago, Mr. Nice explained that this K12 started to testify and then you let him go. I think that I have the right to cross-examine him, at least in relation to -- this is a false witness. This behaviour confirms that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He gave no evidence upon which you could cross-examine. That's why you didn't cross-examine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is Fred Abrahams, and as the Court knows, his evidence will be in fully open session, but as the Court knows, there's an objection from the accused about him and it may be appropriate to hear the objection first. But before -- perhaps it might help Mr. Milosevic and the Chamber to know that the scope of the evidence to be called by that witness is narrower than might appear from the statement. As I explained on Friday, I have no interest in exploring matters of recent history with that witness. I'll just find the summary. I am concerned to explore one or two matters with him that happened in 1998, and of course to deal with the way in which the various reports that he produced were served on the organs of Yugoslav and Serbian authority at the time and indeed on the accused himself. The Chamber may also, it may be, want to hear from him in any event on the means of preparation of the exhibit under orders which is now an exhibit in this case. But I understand that there is a widespread objection based on Mr. Abrahams' work for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just so we can follow this, we have in front of us a summary described as direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's what you would produce?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, you have addressed us on the topic of this witness. You've objected to him. Your objection has been that during two periods, the witness worked for the Office of the Prosecutor, specifically that he worked on this particular indictment. And he said in one statement - I have it - statement of the 24th of January of this year: "I've worked for two short periods as a consultant for the Office of the Prosecutor, from April to June 2000 and again in August 2001. I conducted research and provided analysis for the Kosovo indictment against Slobodan Milosevic et al." So your objection is that he worked on this particular indictment. But it may be -- the point is this -- that he may have done, and obviously that's a matter which you can cross-examine about and it may go to weight, but the question is whether it should prevent him giving evidence about totally different matters or about, rather, the matters which he saw and heard in Kosovo. Yes. If you'd like to address us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that it's all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the same to me what you are going to decide, but you have it stated quite clearly here that from April to June 2000 and yet again in August 2001, as he said, carried out investigations and conducted an analysis for the indictment on Kosovo against Slobodan Milosevic. In other words, Abrahams wrote the indictment. And yet again we encounter the Prosecutor's desire to be both the Prosecutor and to be the witness, to put the questions and to answer the questions. Again, this is one of the closest associates of the OTP in writing the indictment, and this is the author of that book of Human Rights Watch, which was also used as one of the main means for the indictment. I particularly emphasised that we can see that, apart from these dates that are written down here, he says in his statement from April to June 2000 and in August 2001, so even apart from these dates that he mentioned, he -- he worked during those days for the OTP. But in November 2001, he also spoke to Ibrahim Rugova in the capacity of investigator. He concealed that. It's not that he disclosed it. He concealed it. And the question is: How many other activities he has concealed in relation to this false indictment. And also all the other things he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The answer to that is that you can cross-examine him about that. It's a matter which goes to the weight, not whether he should be allowed to give evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been saying that it is so obvious his direct participation in writing the indictment that his entire statement is practically identical to the indictment. That's what I've been referring to. So this statement is supposed to serve for propaganda purposes for the Prosecution for the indictment. As far as I am concerned, you can have anybody you want testify. But I just want to point out what kind of things the other side resorts to when they are trying to do whatever they can in support of their indictment. This man did not take part in anything that is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit this statement. The objection is namely that for the period which I mentioned, the short period that he worked for -- the witness worked for the Office of the Prosecutor and the fact that he worked on this particular indictment does not make his evidence inadmissible. It may be the subject of cross-examination. The accused can ask witnesses -- questions about it of the witness, but it cannot stop him giving evidence. That would be quite wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I've asked the witness to come in. I've asked him to come straight down to court. I hope he will be outside the door. And, Your Honour, I will try to take his evidence shortly so far as I can. I recognise that we are already in a stage of the trial where there is evidence that is potentially repetitive of what's gone before, and I always try and excise what is repetitive unless it's been plainly put in issue so much by the accused that it would seem to merit repetition. Your Honour, I think the witness's statements were subject to the 92 bis procedure. I've worked on the basis that he's not going to be acceptable under those provisions, and I don't know if the Chamber had made any decision, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let us take him as a live witness. I think it's a much matter way to deal with it. While we're waiting, so that we may know what is happening, the next witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are crime-base witnesses, the remaining crime-base witnesses for Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have a note here that in the cases of Mehmeti, Jemini, Elshani and Avdyli, the statements were served after the 11th of February. Therefore, I think technically leave is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm very grateful to you for reminding me of that. I know Ms. Graham was going to give me a note this morning. Time hasn't yet allowed me to pick up on the position. I think it's less unsatisfactory than the Court may fear, but I'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Frederick Cronig Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I'm going to ask you this morning to be as concise in your evidence-in-chief as you can. It may be difficult where you want to give a longer answer to be entirely responsive to the shorter format that my questions will suggest but I would ask you to bear in mind the overall interests of the trial in acheiving brevity. With leave of the Court, I will just lay, by leading questions, your background. You have a Bachelor's degree from Washington University, a Master's in international affairs from Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs, concentrating in Eastern Europe. Did you in due course work for Helsinki Citizens Assembly in Prague between 1990 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you sit forward, then you'll find that the microphones will pick you up. Did you work in Albania at the media training centre of the Soros foundation between 1993 and 1994; following that, five years' work with Human Rights Watch as a researcher and later senior researcher, covering South Balkans with responsibility for Albania, Macedonia, and Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to your work for the Office of the Prosecutor, have you, as a result of your time in Albania, learned the language?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sufficient for conversation but, in your judgement, not for such exercises as taking witness statements and matters of that sort?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I can conduct rudimentary interviews in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've worked for the Office of the Prosecutor once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: On two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: First occasion was April, May, and June 2000. The second was in the month of August 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By what job title did you go when working for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Research analyst was my title.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you also involved in interviewing potential witnesses and in the taking of witness statements?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And have you left your job at Human Rights Watch save for returning for consultancy work, and are you currently engaged in writing a book about Albania?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I left Human Rights Watch in March 2000 before beginning the period here at the Tribunal, and I am currently an occasional consultant. I've done one consultancy for them since leaving as a full-time employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you are writing the book to which I referred?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm currently writing a book about Albania's transition from communism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch is a non-governmental organisation. In a sentence, what does it do?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch monitors and reports on human rights violations around the world. It's a non-governmental organisation that reports without regard for religious, ethnic, or political affiliation, and by mandate we do not accept any government funds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have your reports included reports on the United States of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. America?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Human Rights Watch is very active in reporting about human rights violations in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we turn to paragraph 6 of your summary - that's for the assistance of the Court, don't turn to it for yourself - can you list some of the other countries of which human rights has written critical reports?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, the list is quite long. I think in almost all countries of the world the organisation has been active as well as documenting abuses by non-state actors. In the Balkans, the organisation has a long history. We have issued reports critical of every government in the region; Albania, Macedonia, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Romania. The list is long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How about NATO following the bombing in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the approach in a report of Human Rights Watch to that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, the organisation has been critical of NATO in a number of respects. First, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's enough, I think, to say that you've been critical of them. The detail, if it's relevant, can be adduced later. So far as narrowing the focus to the former Yugoslavia and the documentation of abuses, by what sectors of the former Yugoslavia have -- in respect of what sectors of the former Yugoslavia by ethnicity have critical observations or reports been made?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I would say no government or ethnic group or -- I wouldn't say we criticise ethnic groups, but there has been no force of any of the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia that has been spared our critique. We have published critical reports of Serbian and Yugoslav government forces, of Croatian government forces, Bosnian government forces, as well as the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that I will end up -- because you and I speak the same language -- in this part of your examination I'm going too fast and I must leave a gap between question and answer. Paragraph 5. Human rights methodology, please. Very shortly. Chamber will be familiar with the general proposition, but we just need on the record what the methodology is.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The primary source for the -- of information for the organisation is fieldwork. That is interviews with the victims and witnesses of abuse. We conduct interviews with these people, lengthy, in-depth interviews in a one-on-one setting whenever possible, and we search for corroborative evidence. If someone has had a legal -- is alleging a legal violation, we ask for court records. If they are alleging physical abuse recently, we ask to see scars or bruises. We also collect documents from medical -- medical records, government reports, and so on. Whenever possible, we also try to visit crime scenes or the sites of alleged violations, and we also try to get information from alleged perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 7. When did Human Rights Watch first start working in and in respect of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The work in Kosovo began in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Between then and 2001, how many reports on the area did Human Rights Watch produce?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I believe Human Rights Watch produced 16 reports on Kosovo in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To whom were those reports published in addition to being published perhaps for general consumption?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Hard copy form or even on e-mail.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The reports are issued publicly and are available on the website, although I believe that started in the mid-1990s. But our reports are also sent to the alleged perpetrators. In this case, all of our reports were sent to the Serbian and Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you achieve that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: There are three primary methods. One is a mailing list, by post, that the reports are sent by the mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And would that be -- you say -- you speak of Serbia and Yugoslavia. Would that be sent to an address in Serbia, as it might be?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it would. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that the only way that you'd attempt to contact the authorities?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No. In addition to a mailing list, Human Rights Watch maintains a fax list, as well as an e-mail list, and I am very -- I -- I know for a fact that all of our reports were sent to the accused using all three methods. I personally remember adding his e-mail address to the -- to the e-mail list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He had, at the time, a personal e-mail address?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember it: slobodan.milosevic@gov.yu.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make use of the embassies of these countries as mailboxes in any way?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I don't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the embassies of the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, our reports were also sent to the Yugoslav embassy in Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your first trip to Kosovo was in what year?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The first trip was in summer 1995, but my first research mission was summer 1996, July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a result of that mission, what report was prepared?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I researched and wrote a report entitled "Persecution Persists," which documented a number of issues but primarily the police abuse inflicted by Serbian authorities against ethnic Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to deal with the distribution of these reports individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's always the same method, is it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, always the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, these reports are essentially for reference. I'm not going to take time going through them in detail at the moment. They may, of course, become significant either at this stage or at later stages of the trial, given what we now know about where they were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But this report, Mr. Abrahams, unless there's a particular passage that you can recall as being an apt and extremely concise summary of the report, I'll get to you summarise it verbally from where you are. This report concerned abuses of the type you've spoken of. Any particular passage on the summary that you'd like to put on the overhead projector for us? If not --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Well, I mean, I'm not prepared to have selected one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. It's probably my mistake in respect of this report. Just tell us then its overall effect and we can look at it over one of the intervals, one of the breaks, and see if there's any need to put --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly, the report documents what we considered to be a pattern of discrimination in education, employment, health care, however, the focus of the report is the police abuse. We documented numerous cases of excessive violence by the police, including some deaths in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 188.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following your mission to Kosovo, did you request meetings with government ministries?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: After this trip, yes, I did. I requested meetings with various ministries. I recall the Serbian and Yugoslav Ministries of the Interior as well as the Ministry of Human Rights. And I had a very difficult time getting meetings with these people. I finally succeeded to get a meeting with the Serbian Deputy Minister of Information but I do recall that I had to essentially occupy his office for two hours until he came back and had to meet me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you have produced to us - and we'll be in a position to produce as a single exhibit after the break rather than now, unless you can do it now - the correspondence that you sent to various ministers and people in authority at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are listed on the summary. I'm going to have them put together as a single exhibit and we'll produce them when they've been further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will give it a number now so it remains chronological. It will be number 189; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to ask the witness to deal with the matters between paragraphs 12 and 17 save for paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, we've heard about the educational agreement and electoral matters and that sort of thing, but one thing we haven't heard about is pyramid schemes. Just tell, if you can, from your own knowledge and experience, in a sentence or so what part, if any, they played in the developing history.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, the collapse of the pyramid schemes in early 1997 led to a -- really a dissolution of the state in Albania by March 1997 and the resultant anarchy had a direct impact on Kosovo, specifically the distribution of arms, the fact that perhaps 700.000 small arms were either distributed or looted in Albania. This provided the KLA with a source of weapons that it previously had been denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in your judgement and experience, did this lead to a change in the size of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I think this was a contributing factor but certainly not the defining factor that caused the KLA's rapid explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you then tell us, please, next about the report "Discouraging Democracy"?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This was a report focusing on police violence inside Serbia, essentially Belgrade but a few other cities. In November 1997, there were elections in Serbia and the opposition parties won 14 of the 18 larger cities. The government tried to block the vote, to annul the vote, and this led to massive protests, 88 days of protests by the opposition and by the student movement in Belgrade, very creative and dramatic demonstrations. I documented the police violence that was inflicted against those protesters. This was violence against peaceful demonstrators as well as some journalists covering the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Produce that exhibit, please and lay the first page of the summary on the overhead projector. Coming your way, Mr. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 190.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Lay the front page of it on the overhead projector. The usher will help you. The summary. We'll see how the first page of it would appear to anybody reading it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It starts off with an assertion: "The government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has demonstrated a blatant disregard for human rights." It sets out the electoral abuses reporters had found. And then if we just cast our eyes over it without reading the paragraphs, we come towards the bottom of the page, where it says: "In this way, the European Union has rewarded Yugoslav President Milosevic for doing what he was legally obligated to do in the first place, to recognise the elections without regard for the other human rights violations that are taking place in Yugoslavia. Such concessions squander a prime source of leverage that the international community needs in order to press for urgent improvement in Milosevic's human rights record and his compliance with the Dayton Agreement. "This report deals with the human rights violations that took place in Serbia from November 1996 to September 1997. It does not address violations in the November 1996 elections itself or the government's attempt to change the results since these issues were covered by the OSCE. Nor does it address other serious human rights abuses in Yugoslavia, such as the ethnic Albanians in Kosovo, Muslims in Sandzak, or ethnic Hungarians in Vojvodina." So that's the scope and summary.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I should just say I believe I said before that the elections were in the end of 1997. Obviously I meant November 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have we already got an exhibit number for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, can we go then to your work in 1998, which led to a report, "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo," which documented abuses both by Serbs and Albanians so that, by the time of this report, there was material for you to be critical of Albanians already.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that report is being gathered up ready for production, a word or so about Drenica, please, and what this report covered.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, this report covers a quite spectrum of violations committed by both sides in the conflict, but one of the most egregious violations occurred in the Drenica valley in February and March 1998. The most notorious incident was the attack on the Jashari compound in the village of Prekaz in which more than 50 people lost their lives, the entire Jashari family save for the 11-year-old girl named Besarte. And we documented indiscriminate attacks and excessive force in that incident. We also looked at the violence on February 28th and March 1st in the villages of Likosane and Cirez. For example, the execution of the ten members of the Ahmeti family, the killing of a pregnant woman named Rukije Nebiu --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: -- and on and on. I would just add that I believe those incidents in Drenica were extremely important for the conflict because they radicalised the Albanian population. Up until that point, the KLA was still a disorganised and somewhat mysterious organisation. After the Drenica killings, I believe it was clear that a peaceful resolution to the conflict was no longer available. It -- as I said, it pushed Albanians over the edge. The report has other issues as well I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. A word -- a word about the area around Decan and your interviewing of refugees in Northern Albania, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice and Mr. Abrahams, you are being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. This report also documents what we call the first major government offensive in Kosovo. That was in May 1998 along the border with Albania, around the town of Decan. And definitely the KLA was active in this region. Definitely the KLA was bringing arms and supplies from Northern Albania. And in my estimation, although I'm not a military expert, the government, the Serbian and Yugoslav government attempted to create a cordon sanataire, in other words, clearing the border. And in the process, many violations of international humanitarian law were committed. I interviewed individuals from that area in Kosovo, and I also went to Northern Albania. There were approximately 15.000 refugees in Northern Albania. An estimated 30.000 people also went to Montenegro, according to UNHCR. And we interviewed these individuals in Albania, and we documented a series of violations such as forced expulsions, the destruction of civilian property, indiscriminate attacks that severely impacted civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Because the report can largely speak for itself --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- I'll ask you to deal with two things. We can see that this is now in a booklet form as opposed to just paper form. We can see on the back of it - and I'd like you to put the reverse of it on the overhead projector, please, or I'll get the usher to do so - we can see your website is referred to. Although it was in booklet form, was it possible Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for you to send the entire document to other people's e-mail addresses?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The entire document, no, but the summary, or to be more precise, the press release announcing the release of the report was sent by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The booklet itself or the book itself, was that sent to the various post boxes, as it were, that you've already referred to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And anybody picking this one up, looking at the back of it, and I think its publication date is actually given as October 1998 or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The back of it reads that [as read]: "The report documents serious breaches of international humanitarian law, the rules of war committed in Kosovo from February to early September 1998." But it goes on to make this point [as read]: "The vast majority of these abuses were committed by Yugoslav and Serbian government forces under the command of Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic. Since February, government troops have systematically destroyed civilian property, attacked humanitarian aid workers and committed extrajudicial executions, all of which are violations of the rules of law." But in the next paragraph, it says [as read]: "The Albanian insurgency, known as the UCK or KLA, has also violated the laws of war by taking civilians hostages and committing some summary executions." So that right at that stage, you were reporting on both sides.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 191.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you returned to Kosovo in September and December for further research; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in your trip there in June, had you contacted the secretary for information in Kosovo, the one person I think you had been able to speak to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. During my research in June, I conducted an interview with Mr. Bosko Drobnjak who was representative of the Ministry of Information in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His attitude at that time?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Drobnjak essentially defended the government position. He claimed that the police were fighting terrorists and that their actions were justified. I think the two main points of our conversation were regarding the blockage of humanitarian aid. At that time, the government had blocked the delivery -- had sometimes blocked the delivery of humanitarian aid, both local organisations like the Mother Theresa Society but also international organisations. And when I asked him about this, he claimed that some humanitarian organisations were assisting the terrorists by helping deliver them supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there for one minute before we move on to the next topic. You, of course, had direct knowledge of what Human Rights was doing. Did you also see quite a lot of other non-governmental organisations that were present there at the time?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Of course. In 1998, there were many, many organisations operating in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is an allegation that NGOs assist one side or other to some conflict that they're involved with, is that an unprecedented allegation or is it made from time to time around the world?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Oh, I believe it's not unprecedented, but it was the first time I heard it used in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As an allegation, is it something that you have to take seriously in order to assess the independence either of your own organisation or of other organisations with which you may have contacts?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we would take it very seriously. The one point is that the government never articulated its concrete allegation. They never mentioned an organisation or an incident. And as far as I know, nobody, no humanitarian organisation was ever denied the opportunity to work, was never charged criminally or punished in any way for this allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- course of preparations for the report we've looked at, did you also write letters or send faxes to various Serbian and Yugoslav ministers and ministries with a variety of questions?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. The first was with Mr. Drobnjak in 1998. I submitted to him a list of ethnic Albanians who were missing and asked him for information. He told me that this was outside of his competency. When I returned to New York, I then sent a series of letters by fax to the relevant authorities. I don't recall precisely, but I do know it was sent to the republican and federal Ministries of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to pause you there to save time.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you get any positive response or any response at all from any of this correspondence?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No. We asked a series of questions and received no response from any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have that correspondence consolidated into a single exhibit. It's entirely my oversight that it wasn't in advance done. May it be allocated a provisional number now and I'll produce it after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 192.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, in the course of preparation of this report, did you, and I think you had a colleague Peter Bouchkaert, did you witness anything yourself at firsthand? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to just simply take us to really the major incident or incidents because the Judges really have heard a lot of evidence over this period and we needn't take small matters.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The biggest issue, incident that you saw yourself.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The most serious incident was the killings of September 26th in the village of Gornje Obrinje in the Drenica valley. Twenty-one members of the family Delijaj were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In a few sentences, and it may take us up to the break, I don't know, but in a few sentences can you just summarise what you saw, realising that the Chamber and the accused have the detailed material if there is to be challenge or further exploration.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, when Mr. Bouchkaert and I arrived in Gornje Obrinje on September 29th, as we entered the crime scene, three bodies were being carried by wooden stretcher out for burial. One of them was the 18-month-old Valmir Delijaj. And in the woods were still seven bodies; five women and two children. All of them appeared to have died from -- from head wounds. They were being -- they were in the process of being taken out of the forest for burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your investigations by interview revealed what?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We conducted a very lengthy investigation, and it's clear there was fighting in and around Gornje Obrinje between the KLA and Serbian forces, but it was also very clear to us that the members of the Delijaj family were murdered. It was clear that these were civilians who were hiding in the forest while the fighting was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- whatever happens in respect of the other witness, I will not seek more than the normal break on this occasion. If there's anything arising from him, I'll deal with it on a later occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, would you remember, please, during this and any other adjournments there may be during your evidence not to speak Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to anybody about it until it's over, including members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position about the exhibits is that Ms. Graham and Mr. Triolo, the case manager in trial support, official chap who do terrific work in this case very sensibly suggested to me on Friday that I put all the exhibits in a folder for you, via e-mail, and it's my mistake entirely for not responding to him and I've made for their lives much more difficult and I do apologise for that. But can we, yes, go back to where we were in Gornje Obrinje. Do we have the photographs? They, of course, have to be produced individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: FA17 relates to what you saw in Gornje Obrinje, I think. Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: As I mentioned, when Mr. Bouchkaert and I entered the forest, the villagers were carrying out three bodies. These are two of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 193.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Followed by FA18.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps that will become Exhibit 194.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Word about this when it's on the overhead projector, or word about this, Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Again, there were seven bodies still in the forest in a small gully. This is one of those seven bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, I think, if we look at it, we can actually see two bodies, a body and a head below it, can we not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It does appear that way, but to be honest, I'm not certain it is another body. There were seven bodies there, so it is definitely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: FA19 to become, if it may, Exhibit 195.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 195.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That, I think, is the photograph of --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is one of the children in the gully. It's perhaps a bit difficult to decipher, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a child.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It's a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were there and you photographed or your colleague photographed the child.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. These photographs were taken by Mr. Bouchkaert, but I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think I'm going to -- yes. Very well. The next Exhibit is FA21. These are bloodstains, I think. Just tell us about their significance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 196.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 196. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the same day that we visited Gornje Obrinje, we also visited another village nearby called Golubovac, and the villagers told us that 13 men had been executed in a yard in the village. We interviewed a number of the witnesses, we inspected this scene. This is -- we saw a series of bloodstains along the fence where they said the men had been killed. This is one of those bloodstains. We also observed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we now need, I think, the next exhibit, which is FA22 - thank you very much - to become Exhibit 197.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The area to which you'd been referred by the villagers of Golubovac, and I'll ask you in due course to say how near to or far from the bloodstains you saw this. The significance is pretty obvious, because what we're looking at is shell casings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, those are shell casings. They were approximately three to four metres away from the bloodstains, and I would add one important detail: Fourteen men were lined up for execution, thirteen of them were killed. There was a survivor, a gentleman named Selman Morina, who was in hiding, but we found him. My colleague interviewed him. He gave us a very detailed description of how he survived the execution line-up. He was shot three times, once in the leg and two times in the arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming back in the Chamber's summary and in your memory, just one detail about a place called Plocica.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Plocica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Plocica, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague and I were driving around Drenica on the main road. In fact, we were with a journalist from The New York Times, Jane Perlez, and her photographer, Wade Goddard. We saw a very large convoy of the Yugoslav army leaving Drenica. It was clearly the army, with heavy weapons and tanks. After they left Drenica, we went in and came into the village of Plocica, which was still on fire. We saw, ourselves, the burning of many civilian structures. I remember seeing a food warehouse with melons and grain that was burning. I remember seeing a cow that had been shot in the head. I remember seeing haystacks that were burned or burning, shouldering haystacks that had clearly been lit purposely on fire because the surrounding area around them was not burning. And very important was that we saw no evidence of fighting in the village. There were no pockmarks, no bullet marks on the outside of the buildings. We saw no trenches to indicate the possible presence of the KLA. We saw no shells in the village. I even remember finding a bottle of empty benzine, a bottle that had had benzine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know how near to or far from that was from any of the scenes of damage or destruction by fire?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The bottle, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't recall, but it was in the village amidst this destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You actually took some photographs of burnt haystacks and the like, they're available for the accused if he wants to ask about them but we needn't burden the record with them at this stage. Now just, please, finally tell us the report "A Week of Terror in Drenica."

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: "A Week of Terror in Drenica" was our findings from the Gornje Obrinje killings and the Golubovac killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again - and I hold it up - was it published in the form of a book?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Introduced, please, as Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 198.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Same destination, same post boxes?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Same ability to use e-mail?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. This report was distributed widely and was also reported widely in the press, including the Yugoslav press.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, we look at the -- inside the front, this was actually published in February 1999. Was there any advance publication of that because it related to September 1998 matters?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: A little bit. When we were publishing the previous report, "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo," we -- it was after -- it was October that report was published. So we included a summary of our Gornje Obrinje findings as an appendix in that report. But this report here is the more in-depth and complete research.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, by the time of this report's actual publication in February, Racak had already occurred.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you pursue with this report the same piggyback approach Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that you had done with the previous report and you included a summary of Racak in this report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that there's a report as early as February 1999 actually covering events from September 1998 up to Racak?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed, if we look at the back of it, the first thing that somebody might look at if they received this document in their embassy or their office, and it -- the back simply reads as follows [as read]: "During the last week of September 1998, Serbian and Yugoslav government forces ended their summer-long offensive with a brutal campaign in Kosovo's Drenica region. In the face of a UN Security Council resolution calling for an immediate end to abuses against civilians, government forces committed summary executions, indiscriminately attacked civilians, and systematically destroyed civilian property." It then deals with the Delijaj family at their compound in Gornje Obrinje, the events at a nearby compound, the 13 men in Golubovac, and concludes with a reference to Racak. Of course, these reports set out one way or another your methodology, Mr. Abrahams. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you at the time of publishing these reports and sending them to the authorities to whom they were sent, did you receive any criticism of your work, its method, its conclusions?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We never received a direct criticism, if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive denials of any kind that you can recall, from the accused or from any of those in the authorities to whom these reports were sent?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No, I do not recall receiving denials from the authorities. They might have done so in the press, but I'm not aware of a specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us of your return in December 1998. Did that lead to yet a further report called "Detention and Abuse in Kosovo"?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may not have a copy of that available, but just tell us what the content of that was, in summary.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This was a brief report looking at abuse in detention. Specifically, there were five individuals in a period of 1998 who had lost their lives as a result of abuse in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The report documents due process violations and this violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The pause is because I'm waiting --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have the French around my ears, channel 5, and that's quite a good clue. You can hear the background as to when one can pick up. So that was another report sent in the usual way. February 1999, please. What did you do again?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: In February 1999, I returned to Kosovo to conduct research in general, to stay apprised of the situation, but we were also interested to document the systematic destruction of civilian property. A colleague of mine, a consultant for Human Rights Watch, was conducting research on rape and sexual violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In light of what happened when NATO started bombing, was it possible for you to complete the research into disruption of civilian property?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No. Our priorities changed with the onset of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, however, receive some photographs? We can produce as a collective exhibit, and I'd like your explanation of them, please. These are photographs of bodies and some other photographs. If you'd like to tell us, please, what they amount to, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 199.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can have them on the overhead projector, and we'll go through them. They're numbered. So it's photograph 1 of Exhibit 199, please. It may be that colour will be of more value, if I can make mine available. They've got colour on the original, but I think it will help if we have these in colour. This photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We obtained photographs of the five individuals who were killed in detention. This is one of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom did you obtain these photographs?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: From a local human rights organisation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we simply pass through the -- we can see the bruising there. The next photograph, number 2, shows the back of a dead man and what appears to be bruising. The -- for the next photograph, 3, and just out of respect for any relations, can we just place not the head on the photograph, please. Thank you. The bruising there evident. And the fourth photograph, the back of another with bruising and indeed lines across it. Can you now, please, go to photograph number 5. Just tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is the village of -- this is the village of Lodza, outside of Pec. I believe this photograph was taken in February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The damage self-evident from the photograph. Did you visit this scene yourself?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I took this photograph myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the -- what we can see on the houses consistent with what kind of damage?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Lodza is a particular case. I won't go into the details unless requested, but the KLA was present in Lodza, but this was -- there are two times when the village was destroyed. On the second occasion, heavy machinery was used to knock out the pillars of the homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Actually, to an extent these photographs, although they show damaged property, give a reasonable impression of the compound format of Kosovo Albanian homes, don't they?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This could be considered typical, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you've got the large house with the height of wall that typically surrounds a compound, I think. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I would consider that fair, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph, please, number 6.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is also a home. It was in fact the only home in Lodza that was left standing. Villagers told us that it was used as a base for Serbian forces. And if I'm not mistaken, the graffiti says, "Cafe flat Lodza" on the left. And on the right, if I'm not mistaken, it says, "Roasted pork," which is obviously an offence to those of the Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The damage to -- sorry, I'm going too fast. The damage to this building, no suggestion of fire damage or is there? We can't really tell from the photograph.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No. I believe this building was not substantially damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Because the history was that it had been used by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That was my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereas when we come to the following photograph, number 7, same or different village?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Now, this is on the road outside of Suva Reka. We took this photograph -- I took this photograph because I thought it explained it. It displayed very clearly the destruction of a private home. Notice the chimneys are still standing, and there are black smoke streaks from the windows. This suggests that these homes were burned from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 8, please, and it's significance.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is clearly the destruction of a mosque. I must admit that I am not sure in which village this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it a photograph taken by you and your colleague? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is again in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. Although this photograph might have been taken in December 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We'll put a question mark over that. But in any event, before NATO bombing, because you left, of course, then. Minarets destroyed in the way this one is.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Without question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Photograph 9.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Again I'm afraid I'm not entirely certain, but I believe this is a photograph from Gornje Obrinje, September. No. I correct myself. The snow there could not make that possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it one of your photographs?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Destruction of a house. And then --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- photograph 10 purpose -- and 11, really, purpose obvious.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reasonably certain this is the Gornje Obrinje mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at photograph 11, we can see some signs of damage on the minaret. Were you able at the time to ascertain more particularly what sort of damage there was there?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, as you can see, the top of the minaret had been destroyed and -- as had the roof, and the inside of the mosque had been -- had been vandalised or gutted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Let's move on, then, to deal with, I think, fleetingly really because of the quantity of material the Judges have from elsewhere, did Human Rights Watch deal with Racak as an individual incident?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not via yourself but by someone else?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It was a Human Rights Watch consultant named Gordana Igric.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know how long or short was her inquiry into Racak?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Her inquiry lasted approximately one week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was a report prepared?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a mini report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if the people wanted, if people were going to be looking at the material on Racak, there is a short Human Rights Watch report called "Yugoslav Government War Crimes in Racak," which is a sort of paper report --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm holding it up now. May we just produce that again so it's there for reference, if necessary, as Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to begin to suggest at the moment that we should look at it for its conclusions, given the degree to which we have firsthand information available. It may assist the accused or others in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The NATO bombing started, Mr. Abrahams. What did that cause Human Rights Watch workers to do?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The organisation immediately sent researchers to the region. On March 28th, the first researcher arrived in Macedonia, and the next day, someone arrived in Northern Albania. We had a research presence on the ground throughout the entirety of the bombing campaign with the aim of interviewing refugees as they left Kosovo, or after they left Kosovo, to document the abuses that we believed were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, can you give the Chamber any idea of the numbers of people who were interviewed by Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Between March 28, 1999 and December 1999, we interviewed approximately 600 ethnic Albanians in relation to Serbian and Yugoslav crimes. That is the people we interviewed during the bombing campaign and those we interviewed inside Kosovo after the bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you perhaps now to deal fairly comprehensively with the methodology for the book "Under Orders" that was produced, but before I come to that as a discrete topic, we've already heard here from a witness called Patrick Ball, and I think that his work and yours connect in some way, and perhaps you'd just like, in a sentence, to set out the history so we can have it in its context.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Sure. I was familiar with Patrick's work regarding statistics in human rights and was one of the people who encouraged him to conduct research regarding the Kosovo crisis, which he did. After we had collected 600 interviews, I also realised that Human Rights Watch's data could be of use, that we might also conduct some statistical analysis using our own data. Dr. Ball assisted us by helping to construct the database and conceive of an approach. Beyond that, there were a host of other statisticians and consultants who assisted us with the actual coding of the data as well as the analysis of the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Dr. Ball was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, we may find, if we look at it in detail, that there are graphs in the book "Under Orders" - for example, at pages 424 and 427 - which have features of similarity to the graphs that were produced by Dr. Ball. In a sentence, is this simply because you were doing the same exercise as Dr. Ball or not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The similarity, in my opinion, is a result of the data on the ground. Our graphs stem from the findings of 600 interviews. It's a Human-Rights-Watch-only data set. Dr. Ball's data set was much broader, much, much broader, and we believe the similarities were striking and very powerful in their evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With that necessary preliminary explanation, can you give us the methodology for the preparation of the book "Under Orders" and indeed the time scale for its production?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The methodology is a bit complex so please tell me to skip anything of irrelevance. First, the background sections of the report are based on our research from 1990 until February 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that include your own published reports and also the balance of the material when you prepared those reports?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. We did not conduct fresh research for those background sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The bulk of the report "Under Orders" is based on our interviews during the NATO bombing and after the NATO bombing. As I mentioned, 600 interviews with ethnic Albanians. This is the crux of the report. There are, however, two other important sections - I consider them very important - which is the research conducted after the NATO bombing. First of all, it is the chapter entitled "Abuses After June 12, 1999" which documents violations and abuses against non-ethnic Albanians, primarily Serbs and Roma.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And primarily by whom?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: These are violations committed by ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The other chapter is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That can be found at page 453, I think.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Page 453, yes. The other important chapter is on 437, "The NATO Air Campaign." In August 1999, Human Rights Watch conducted an investigation inside Yugoslavia to determine the civilian impact or the impact on civilians that the NATO bombing had. We issued a report about that. We also -- during the NATO bombing, Human Rights Watch criticised NATO's use of cluster bombs which we consider to be an indiscriminate weapon. And the findings of those two reports are summarised in "Under Orders," that is, our criticisms of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you speak of the interviews with 600 people, can you give us an idea of the scope of any such interview; its duration, its time constraints, and so on? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: In general, the interviews are lengthy. There may -- there were times certainly when refugees were literally coming across the border in a tractor and there was not time for much more than, "Where are you from? When did you leave, and why did you leave?" But usually the interviews are in-depth, they're lengthy, and they're one-on-one. We always try to conduct our interviews in a one-on-one setting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your criticism of the KLA or of Kosovo Albanians, was there anything unprecedented in your preparing and publishing a report on this topic? Were you the first people to do it or had others done it before you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Regarding Kosovo, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe we were the first. Other -- I don't recall who was actually the first in documenting these abuses, but certainly other human rights organisations were also active in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I then ask you about a different report called "Abuses Against Serbs and Roma in the New Kosovo." When was that published and was that in any sense a breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Immediately after the NATO bombing ended and NATO forces entered Kosovo on June 12th, Human Rights Watch began to monitor abuses by Albanians against non-ethnic Albanians. We issued our first statement, if I'm not mistaken, on June 16th. We issued a number of statements after that, critical of these revenge attacks. And we published a large report in August 1999 which, if I'm not mistaken, was the first such report from a major human rights organisation to criticise and denounce these -- these abuses; specifically harassment, beatings, expulsions, arson --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: -- and killings. And killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we put the front page of this, in line with previous practice, on the overhead projector, you can see how the reader --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 201.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- how the reader would see what was likely to be within. It's set out extremely clearly the following: "A wave of arson and looting of Serb and Roma houses throughout Kosovo has ensued since KFOR's entry into the province. Serbs and Roma who remained have been subjected to harassment and intimidation, including severe beatings. Most seriously, there's been a spate of abductions and murders of Serbs since mid-June, including the massacre of 14 Serb farmers on July 23." Same destinations, same post boxes, or did you manage to find anyone who -- so let me break that question into two. Same basic post boxes?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to send this to anybody representing the Kosovo Albanian side?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It was distributed, first of all, to all the media in Kosovo. It was distributed to all the international organisations, to all of the ethnic Albanian political parties, and it was also given to what was at that time called the provisional government of Kosovo. This was a government established for a brief period of time. And I personally delivered a batch of these reports to that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other report that I'd like you to deal with in just a little more detail is called "Rape as a Weapon of Ethnic Cleansing." Can you tell us a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. After -- after the NATO bombing, a series of researchers came into Kosovo. We had a continuous presence. A researcher named Benjamin Ward was in Kosovo almost continuously. But another researcher named Martina Vandenberg, who is an expert on rape and sexual violence, came to Kosovo to conduct investigations. She documented 96 cases of rape or sexual violence against ethnic Albanians committed by Serbian or Yugoslav forces during the period of the armed bombing -- of the NATO, NATO bombing. But I would emphasise, as the report does, that these 96 cases in no way represent the full magnitude of this problem. It was very obvious that the number is larger, primarily on account of the social taboo connected with crimes of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
