utterances.text: Can you explain, because you've been in Kosovo and speaking the Albanian language to the degree you do, can you explain to the Chamber, possibly even in ways that women, were any to be called, might feel it not possible to do, what the taboo is and what the consequence is of even being discovered to be a victim spoken to by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Clearly there is a social stigma connected with crimes of this nature to the extent that women, Albanian women, might not be able to find a husband if it's known that they had been a victim of sexual crime. Or in the very least, viewed in a very negative way by the society. It's an unfortunate reality, but it is a traditional place. So it was clear to us that many women did not want to come forward. And those who did wanted -- requested anonymity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The pattern of sexual violence in the course of these events, is there anything that you would like to comment upon? The summary on the front page of this particular report doesn't amount to a summary but the title is, "as a Weapon of Ethnic Cleansing." Could you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Our conclusion was that sexual violence was not an isolated incident. It occurred in a variety of locations over a period of time. We felt that it was, unfortunately, common practice. Essentially, it took three general forms: Either rapes in private homes, which is when a security force would enter a home and assault a woman; secondly, rapes in flight, meaning as Albanians were leaving Kosovo, they would be stopped and taken out of a convoy, sexually abused; or thirdly, what we've called rapes in detention, where women were actually held in a location and sexually abused. We've documented all three categories of abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could we have an exhibit number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 202.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the larger report which we've been considering, "Under Orders," wasn't actually published until when?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: October 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With these other smaller reports coming out in the meanwhile?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. And many of those smaller reports are summarised essentially, with some updates, in "Under Orders."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The conclusions of "Under Orders," of course can speak for themselves for those who read or refer to the book, but paragraph 46 of the summary, the killings and their part, if any, in the overall operation, how was that regarded?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we documented 3.453 killings, but this is based on the 600 interviews. Clearly, this number 3.400 does not represent the total. The killings, in our opinion, very briefly, can be broken into three general categories. One was to expedite the cleansing process, which means a few killings in a village to incite fear and encourage the population to leave. The second category of killings is what we've called targeted killings. These are politicians, human rights activists, prominent individuals in the community. And I would highlight here the killings on March 24th of the human rights lawyer Bajram Kelmendi along with his two sons Kastriat and Kushtrim. Or the murder in April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence about these incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the third motivation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The third motivation would be revenge. And there are cases where the KLA or Albanians killed Serbian forces and, a few days afterwards, there was a large-scale killings that might have been connected with the previous incident. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to deal with 50, 51, 52. We've had evidence of that. Fifty-three of the summary may help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any geographical -- did you see any points of geographical significance --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in the abuses?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: In our opinion, the areas hardest hit in Kosovo were the areas where the KLA was most active, and in fact, five municipalities - which are Srbica, Glogovac, Orahovac, Suva Reka, and now I'm forgetting the fifth. Orahovac, Suva Reka, and Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Sixty-five per cent of the violations we documented took place in these areas -- in these five municipalities. However, there were clearly serious crimes committed in areas where the KLA was not active. The municipality of Lipljan is a good example, or villages such as Cuska in the Pec municipality. Areas of Istok municipality where KLA activity was minimal but expulsions and killings nevertheless took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've dealt already, I think, with the statistical point that I wanted to make. You can be asked further about that, if necessary. As to paragraph 57, "Chain of Command," If you can just help us with that, please. Were you, from your researches - and you're not, as you said, a military expert - were you able to say anything about chains of command?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We conducted our research using open sources, specifically the magazine Policajac, which is the official journal of Ministry of Interior, Serbian ministry, as well as the magazine Vojska, official publication of the Yugoslav army, and the website of the Serbian MUP. These provided us with a great deal of information that helped us to construct pieces of the chain of command as it related to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, the conclusions are stated in the report. We've, I believe, accurately reconstructed the chain. The Yugoslav army chain was clearer, was more clear. Specifically, I think we recognised in the Ministry of Interior a divergence from de facto and de jure structures. In other words, the -- the legal structure of the Ministry of Interior is not always how it happened in the field. That was our impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, what is your base in determining the -- when you're mentioning the de jure chain of command? Is it based on the interviews you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That's based on the public records, the open sources that we collected, such as the magazines, which listed the -- occasionally listed the reporting structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. De facto chain of command, did the open sources include these materials in connection with the de facto command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. An example I can provide is the role of Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic, who is not officially in the legal structure but, through media reports and through my work in Kosovo, it was very obvious that he played a prominent role in political negotiations and in Kosovo politics in general. So perhaps that's an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wasn't he the chairman of the cooperation committee with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he was involved in negotiations. I'm not certain of that position precisely. But speaking about the Serbian chain, he does not have an official place in that structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Court can find, can they not, the wiring diagrams, as they're called, for the army and the MUP on pages 68 and 77 as you felt able, or you and your co-authors felt able to describe the position?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do they show the basic structures of the army and the MUP as you and your co-authors felt able to record them?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again, I'm not going to take you through them in detail, but this I do want, and this comes from another source, I think. What did you find, if anything, from your field research about the interaction of the MUP and the army?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, our interviews revealed what we considered to be a very high level of coordination, which means that the army and the police, as well as local militia groups or paramilitaries seems to be acting in cooperation or conjunction with one another. Typically, the army or the special police would surround a village and shell from a distance, followed by the entrance into the village by police as well as local militia. At this point, the separation and interrogation of men would occur as well as lootings and, in some cases, also killings. But it was clear to us that -- that there was a coordination. Of course, there were incidents where coordination was less effective, but that is our overall impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paramilitaries, in summary. How did they feature in the 600 interviews that you conducted and analysed?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, in our opinion, the paramilitaries in Kosovo were different from previous conflicts in Bosnia or Croatia. Rather than operating independently, or rather than operating as separate groups - for example, Arkan's unit - they were more integrated into the official structures. So they would be integrated into a local police force or the special police, rather than operating as separate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That leaves me with the two outstanding clips of correspondence and three other exhibits that I ought to produce. Can I deal with the exhibits first and then the correspondence? Paper 4. I said I wouldn't produce the photographs of the haystacks partly because the ones I saw last week were less clear than these, but perhaps we can just trouble you with these for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They will become Exhibit 200 and --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 203.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These are, I think, photographs that you've taken yourself and which do depict a reality. Just remind us when they were taken.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This photograph is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll try and get a colour one on the overhead projector for the wider audience to see.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is a photograph taken on September, I believe 27th of 1998, of Plocica village. This is the food supply building where we saw melons and flour burning inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the whole building seems to have been destroyed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The building is on fire. I don't know if the photograph shows it, but flames are still inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, we can see those. And then the second photographs here is the characteristic haystacks in the background.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is again Plocica village on the day I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's the stacks in the foreground. Yes?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I said we didn't have the report "Detentions and Abuse in Kosovo" which was published in December 1998. In fact, we do have it, and perhaps I can just produce that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 204.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we look -- thank you very much. And if we look because it's a paper report and not a printed one in the sense, if we look at the second sheet, Mr. Abrahams, which I'll ask to be placed on the overhead projector so we can see how the media would pick up what this was all about. The report says straight away that [as read]: "Since the armed conflict began in late February 1998, at least 1.200 ethnic Albanians have been charged under Serbian law with terrorism or anti-state activities" and so on. And then the next paragraph [as read]: "Physical abuse and torture of detainees is widespread. Five individuals are known to have died..." and so on, and then it goes on to deal with matters in detail. Yes?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The last but one report on the same general topic is a much earlier report which we haven't looked at, and it's called "Human Rights Abuses in Kosovo" and is dated 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: March 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 205.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe we can look at the back of this and simply put that on the overhead projector to see what a recipient would make of it. Human Rights Watch as long ago as 1993 was saying this [as read]: "Kosovo is a police state. Police raids on homes and marketplaces occur daily and Serbian authorities have stepped up a drive to push Albanians out of Serbian-populated areas. Heavily armed Serbian police, paramilitary groups, and regular army forces spread their terror. Mass arrests of Albanians on trumped-up charges are commonplace and, in a society run by brute force and intimidation, few prisoners ever receive a fair trial." It goes on to deal with the content of the report. Now, your involvement at that time was, I think, with Human Rights Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Watch nil, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I was not working at Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was prepared by others. Do you know to whom this was published at the time?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: You mean to whom it was distributed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To whom it was distributed and in that way published, yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: My understanding is that all reports were sent to the relevant authorities in Belgrade, but not having been present at the organisation at that time, I cannot testify for sure to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. Exhibit number already given. Thank you. Your Honour, the last report that Mr. Abrahams could produce is the one on "Civilian Deaths in the NATO Air Campaign." That, of course, is not part of our case but it's relevant, but Chamber has expressed an interest in the topic and has allowed the accused to cross-examine on it. It just seems, for completeness, that ought to be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 206.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you've told us that you were critical of NATO. Here's the report that was produced. If we go to the -- I think it's the third -- the second sheet, on the reverse side, we come to something called the summary. This is not -- there is not a front or back cover. It deals with the summary. You see: "Summary and Principal Findings," which is: "Minimising harmed civilians was central to governmental and public consent to NATO's bombing campaign." And then we go on: "From the beginning of Operation Allied Force --" next paragraph --" NATO and allied government military officials stressed their intent to limit casualties." And then third paragraph: "Despite precautions ..." and so on, it then goes on: "Human Rights Watch has conducted a thorough investigation of civilian deaths as a result of NATO action. On the basis of this investigation, Human Rights Watch has found that there were 90 separate incidents involving civilian deaths during the 28-day bombing campaign. Some 500 Yugoslav civilians are known to have died in these incidents." Yes?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may be asked further questions about this by the accused, but would you be in a position to summarise in a few sentences the effect of this report or is it better to let it speak for itself in due course?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: How do you mean the effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The effect. Is there anything -- the opinion of Human Rights Watch on the NATO deaths.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I can only say this: This number, 500, was much lower than the estimates given by the Yugoslav government, but it was also considerably higher than the numbers given by NATO and NATO governments. And I consider this a very good sign of the report's objectivity. I can also say I thought that conducting this report was critical. I that it was necessary to investigate the allegations, the serious allegations against NATO, and that no force in this conflict be left uncritiqued or at least uninvestigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Two exhibits, bundles of correspondence, please. The first one in time is Exhibit 189, original and copies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 207.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is 189.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 189. We've already reserved a number for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think, Mr. Abrahams, you regard one of these letters as containing a mistake by you, which we better identify straight away. We will come to that in a second.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the clip of correspondence, this is 1996, we see your sending a letter first to Mr. Mirovic, requesting a meeting with government officials when you're next in Belgrade. You talk about terrorist violence. If we go to the next letter, it's a letter to Minister Jokanovic about recent terrorist violence. The next one to Mrs. Gordana at the Ministry of Human Rights in Yugoslavia. Any reply from her?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No. I was not granted meetings with any of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see the only acknowledgement you received, I think, in the fax sheet that follows. Explain that, please. Sorry. It's not a fax from anybody else.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I believe it's this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Explain that.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This, I am so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Beg your pardon? Just explain --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Is that what you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. No, the one that says, Sorry about the basketball, congratulations on the silver.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. After my meeting with Rade Drobac, the Deputy Minister of Information, the ministry promised that they would provide information to me on 16 ethnic Albanians who were missing. I followed up in New York by sending a fax. This is Dragan Milosevic, I believe no relationship to the accused, who worked -- was -- worked in the Ministry of Information. I sent him a fax with my questions, and then this is -- seems comical now, but as a friendly gesture on my cover sheet I said, please, I'm sending you my questions, and at the time, the US basketball team had just beaten the Yugoslav team in the Olympics, so I had --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that was the total of the reply from him. If we come back in the bundle to your letter to him of the 31st of July, the second sheet of it, I think in paragraph 1 you recognise that -- you defended, really, Human Rights Watch's own or your own protocols in the use of terminology. Second sheet. Next page, please. Where it says: "Please update."

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. These are the questions that I submitted to the Ministry of Information. The error and the mistake I believe is in question number -- in point number 1. We ask for information on recent terrorist attacks, and I -- I regret using that term in subsequent reports we avoided using that phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How does Human Rights Watch adjust its -- or how does it use language consistent with its aim of being objective to all participants --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in any conflict?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The organisation is very cautious to avoid what we would call politically loaded terms, terms that are imprecise and open for interpretation. "Terrorist" is one of those terms. "Regime" is another term. Or emotional words like -- like -- like perhaps "massacre." Better for the KLA - and what we used in the future - would be "an armed insurgency," "guerilla army" or "a rebel army"; something that is more neutral and descriptive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second clip of correspondence and the last, therefore, to be dealt with is the 1998 correspondence, already exhibited as --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 192. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This contains the letters that you sent to the Minister of Justice, Markicevic, on the 20th of July 1998, asking for help. And it's quite interesting to see the questions. You ask about how many ethnic Albanians are currently in police detention, how many have been charged with criminal offences, what are the charges against a particular individual or the whereabouts of certain persons, and you then ask if they can provide evidence of human rights abuses against ethnic Serbs, civilians, police, or VJ soldiers, such as false detentions or killings. Can you just explain the format of the questions you were asking, the strategy, if there's a strategy, behind it all at that time?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This was in preparation for the report "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo," and we sought to represent the situation as realistically as possible. We sought input from the government on these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. issues as matters of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that the first four topics appear to relate to things that may have been suffered by Albanians but the last topic specifically raises the issue of the reverse, of --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- problems that may have been caused by ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: As the opening sentence states, or the second sentence, I suppose, the report will document abuses by all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Any reply to that letter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No reply, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nor to the one to the Ministry of Justice on the following page?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yugoslav Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or to the Serbian Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which is now a differently phrased set of questions but time doesn't justify our going through all of them. To the Secretary of Information, Mr. Goran Matic?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a fax cover sheet. You wrote actually to the magazine which you've told us was one of your sources of open source information.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is a letter to the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, it's to the army itself. And this address that you chose, can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely where I obtained this address, but I know that I had a telephone book that I obtained while in Belgrade and most likely I took this address from -- from that telephone book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, the Serbian Secretary for Information and the Yugoslav Ministry of the Interior. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the only questions I ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The case managers were right that a binder would have been helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Entirely my oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't suppose one has been prepared at all, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think it has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall seek, at some stage, just five minutes to deal with the previous witness, an update on the position. Probably better if I do it after the break rather than before, but I'm in your hands whether then or at the end of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be most convenient at the end of the morning rather than interrupt. We'll adjourn now and take the 20-minute break. What would be helpful sometime, speaking for myself, would be an indication of Drenica on the map. It's frequently used and never very clear on the various maps I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not immediately, but at some stage it would be helpful to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think there will be any difficulty in getting this witness to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it may not be the appropriate witness, it may be sensible to get someone who has an overall view. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You wrote in your statement - that is the second statement you gave - that from April to June 2000, that you worked for the OTP, and then again in August 2001. That is to say, the first time round for three months and the other time for one month. And you also said that you worked on investigations and that you did an analysis for the indictment on Kosovo against me. What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The question is what did I do while working for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here, as I quoted to you, that you did an analysis for the indictment against me. What does that mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: While working for the Prosecutor, I had two tasks. The first was to contact and interview what I would call the political personalities of Kosovo; individuals who were involved in political activity or specifically negotiations of one form or another. The other task was the collection of documents, specifically to collect documents of the Serbian police or Yugoslav army or other relevant documents to help explain the activities of the government in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But what does the word "analysis" mean? You are not talking about collecting facts. You say that you made an analysis. What does that actually mean?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: My job was to identify the political personalities among the Kosovo Albanians who could potentially contribute to this case. So in that regard, a degree of analysis was required to determine whether an individual played a role, what role they played, and if they could somehow contribute. The same goes for the documents, to better understand -- to understand whether a document is relevant requires some analysis. Although I did much less of this, I actually collected everything I could get my hands on and left the analysis to the experts here in the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of this activity of yours, do you consider yourself to be one of the co-authors of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No, I do not, in no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your cooperation on the analysis and collection of data for the indictment does not qualify you as one of the co-authors of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's just said that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that from April to June 2000 and in August 2001 were the only times when you worked for the OTP. However, it can be seen here that you also worked for the Office of the Prosecutor in the capacity of investigator when on the 1st of November and 3rd of November, 2001, which is outside this particular time period that you mentioned as your periods of engagement in the OTP, you conducted interviews with Ibrahim Rugova. Why did you remain silent on that particular engagement for the Office of the Prosecutor, which I believe is not being doubted in any way?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: First of all, I was never an investigator for the Tribunal. I was a research analyst. Secondly, the answer to your question is actually quite simple. When I worked at the Tribunal in August 2001, I ended up leaving The Hague, leaving the job, two days early. I had to return to New York. In October 2001, I was in the region. I was in Kosovo and then I went to Albania for research on my book. And because I had two days left on my contract and the bureaucracy at the Tribunal was concerned about that, and also because I wanted to continue the work that I had started, I offered, while in Kosovo, to assist specifically with the interview with Dr. Rugova. I was the person, together with the investigator Jonathan Sutch who initially contacted Dr. Rugova in August and spoke with him about the possibility of giving a statement. And at the end of October, beginning of November, Dr. Rugova was ready. I was in Kosovo. I had two days on my contract that I promised to fulfil, so I agreed, together with Jonathan Sutch to conduct this interview, in other words, to take the statement that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have two contracts with the Office of the Prosecutor, one for this period of three months from April until June and the other one for the month of August?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How much did they pay you for that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to recall precisely. I had what's known as a GTA contract. I know that my rank was P3. And if I remember correctly, the salary is somewhere between 1.500 and 2.000 dollars a month, but I would have to check my records to be certain of that. The P3 salary, I believe, is public record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of this that you spoke of today and the documents that you enclosed, these booklets, et cetera, as far as I understood, you did within your activities in the Human Rights Watch organisation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that this organisation is an impartial, objective organisation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since you mentioned this in your statement, as you spoke of the NATO bombing, is the bombing of civilian targets a crime?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch had determined from its research that NATO violated international humanitarian law, and I can explain where and how, if that is of interest. However, the organisation did not conclude that NATO had committed war crimes, and the distinction there, in brief, is the notion of criminal intent. That while the organisation criticised NATO for some of its targeting, we did not have conclusive evidence to prove that NATO specifically and purposefully targeted civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when you have information about targeted hospitals, buses, railroads, you put Aleksinac on the first page - this is a small mining town in the centre of Serbia - do you really not consider these to be civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The issue here is NATO's selection of targets, and whether there was a military legitimacy in these targets. Again, our conclusion was that very serious concerns were raised. We criticised NATO for not taking enough measures to minimise the civilian casualties, not taking enough measures to adequately distinguish between civilian and military targets. And we also criticised the use of cluster bombs, which we consider to be an indiscriminate weapon. I should note that in May, the White House issued a directive stopping the use of cluster bombs, but they were used up to that point. Given that, however, we did not collect enough evidence to convincingly prove that civilian targets were chosen with the specific intent of injuring or killing civilians. And our burden of proof is high. We have the same burden of proof for all of our research, and without having the conclusive evidence, we were not prepared to make the allegations that war crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When bearing in mind, for example, that cluster bombs were used to bomb the centre of the city of Nis, does that mean that these are civilian targets and that there cannot be sufficient proof that cluster bombs were thrown in the centre of Nis, near the market, the clinics, the university? Is there a trace of doubt in your mind with regard to this?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The report Human Rights Watch issued, of which I helped edit but did not research, called on the NATO governments, or called on NATO itself to investigate, to establish a commission to investigate what we considered serious allegations. NATO did not do this. At least, not publicly yet. And the cluster bomb incident in Nis that you mention is, without question, one of the issues -- one of the incidents that deserves further investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the use of depleted uranium, is that a crime?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm not a legal expert. I'm not a lawyer, so I'm hesitant to give a definitive answer to that. Certainly one of the fundamental principles of the Geneva Conventions is minimising the impact war has on civilians. So depleted uranium could perhaps be viewed in that context, but that's a legal argument that I'm not -- I'm not qualified to -- to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Abrahams. As far as I can understand this, if I can make the proper conclusion on the basis of what you've said, in response to the question as to whether the targeting of civilian targets is a crime or not, whether the use of cluster bombs is a crime or not, whether the use of depleted uranium is a crime or not, are questions that you cannot give a precise yes or no answer to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No, that's not exactly right. Clearly, many of those issues you mentioned are specific crimes if they are done in full knowledge that they are crimes and if they are done with the aim of arming civilians. And our conclusions did not reach that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, in response to a question that puts together all the three that I have put to you as examples, the aggression of NATO, is it against the charter of the UN or not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that part of your expertise or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, not a question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. That is a very logical reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now, we have mentioned a few examples that are characteristic of the NATO aggression. You mentioned in your statement many crimes that were committed by the so-called KLA. In all fairness, the numbers were diminished, but they are still impressive enough, even the ones that you mentioned. You mentioned 250.000 expelled Serbs, you mentioned 1.000 killed persons, you mentioned 1.000 persons who were abducted, although that is far below the actual figure. You did not mention tens of thousands of burned Serb houses or many other things. But at least what you mentioned, do you consider that to be a crime?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: First of all, I would make a brief correction. You mentioned a thousand killed and a thousand missing. In fact, that is the same figure. There are a thousand Serbs and Roma who have gone missing after the NATO intervention, after June 12th, and many of them are feared dead. But I don't want to make 1.000 into 2.000. In answer to your question, yes, we consider those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now that we bear in mind the crimes that were committed by NATO, and you don't have this spelled out very precisely, and then we have these crimes that were committed by the KLA where you were quite categorical, how come Human Rights Watch or you personally did not accuse the perpetrators of those crimes before this institution, although it is an illegal institution, just as you accuse me, for example, or the Serb army, police, et cetera? How come you omitted to do that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: On numerous occasions, we called for full accountability. We've called on the Tribunal to investigate in an impartial manner, crimes committed by all sides, we've documented crimes committed by all sides, or violations, and we have called for accountability for the crimes committed by the Kosovo Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again you are talking about impartiality and objectiveness. Do you really think that what you have enclosed here now, that -- this that has to do with NATO aggression, where underneath the photograph on page 1, there is a caption saying "Three civilians killed in Aleksinac," and then inside, you say in your statement that 500 were killed, and you know that it is not three civilians, you know it is not 500; you know the figures are much bigger. All have been registered in official documents. Doesn't it seem to you that this is an intentional minimising of the effect of the crime that was committed against my country precisely by your organisation Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I believe that the figures in this report are accurate. They are much less than what the Yugoslav government was saying, and they are also much higher than what NATO admitted. But perhaps the best evidence comes from the Belgrade District Court, because in August 2000, a case was heard in Belgrade against the NATO leaders accusing Clinton, Blair, Wesley Clark, and so on. And in the indictment submitted by the Belgrade prosecutor, the number of civilians killed by NATO is approximately 500. We've compared the document, the indictment, with our report, and a few of the names are different. They have some we don't have, we have some they don't have. But the number is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is my impression that you didn't read those facts and figures properly, but let's leave that to one side. You're, therefore, claiming that Human Rights Watch and the efforts made by the Human Rights Watch were objective ones, impartial ones, and well-intentioned ones; is that right? That would be, as a whole, your approach; right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that. I believe we made every effort to be as objective as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there are people who are objective and impartial working there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I believe the level of professionalism is very high.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you bear in mind everything that you can take off the site and when you see the composition of the Human Rights Watch organisation, you can see Warren Zimmermann, for example, the former US ambassador who, among other things, is well known for saying to Alija Izetbegovic to reject the Lisbon Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've been told before to keep the questions short. Now, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as the witness is claiming that the Human Rights Watch is an objective organisation, my question to him is as follows: How can he consider it to be objective when, inside it, the person giving him his job is George Soros, Abramowitz is Thaci's advisor in Rambouillet, within it we have Mr. Zimmerman who advised Izetbegovic to reject the Lisbon Agreement, that is to say people who are profoundly and deeply involved in American policy and politics and who came out in favour of the bombing of Yugoslavia, the aggression against Yugoslavia, in addition to many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you claim this to be true or not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I need to make a point of clarification. It is not accurate to say that these individuals like Warren Zimmermann and Morton Abramowitz are in Human Rights Watch. What is accurate is that both of those individuals are members of the advisory committee of the Europe and Central Asia division where I worked. The advisory committee has a specific function, namely, as its name implies, to give advice. They are present as experts in the region who give us input to help prioritise our work, but they do not in any way have an executive function. They are not involved in research, they do not review our findings. And I can state personally through my work that I never had a conversation with either of those individuals. We might add there also Herb Okun, another former US diplomat. I never had a conversation with them about my concrete findings or how to present my concrete findings. I should also stress that, in terms of prioritising our work, we definitely didn't need any expert to tell us that we should concentrate on Kosovo. That was obvious from the facts. And lastly -- well, two quick points: One is these individuals you mentioned are no longer holding official positions. In fact, the advisory committee members are not allowed to hold official positions at the same time. And lastly, regarding Human Rights Watch's objectivity, the best evidence or the strongest argument I can provide is the work. Looking at Kosovo, I've spoken today about the reports we did. Looking at the region, the Balkans, we've documented abuses by all sides in the conflict. I personally began my career in Albania and published three reports that were very critical of the Albanian government. And the organisation as a whole is active in more than 80 countries around the world, including the United States. So I believe the catalogue of reports is evidence enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But don't you feel that if we take into consideration all this, everything that we've been talking about in this short space of time, that the role of the Human Rights Watch was to produce alibis for interference into the internal affairs of other countries? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said you began your career in Albania and that you were doing research into the violations of rights of the Greek minority. Well, did you draw any arguments there, sufficient argumentation to see the way in which and for how long - let me say for several decades, in fact, and systematically so, in the harshest possible way - rights were violated and the Greek minority in Albania even destroyed. Did you draw these facts and those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: My findings were quite different. I did conclude and I did document a series of violations, enough to fill a report. And in fact, my first report for Human Rights Watch was on human rights violations against the Greek minority in Albania. I'm happy to elaborate on the details if the Court deems it relevant, but I did not conclude that those violations were anywhere near as extreme as the violations being committed in Kosovo. There were problems with education, there was a prominent court case, but there wasn't the persistent systematic and ongoing violence that we documented in Kosovo. In no what I could I compare the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did violence exist against Kosovo Albanians of the type that you're talking about, that is to say, any kind, any kind of violence before, prior to the terrorists started killing -- their killings after 1960 -- 1996, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're asking about prior to 1960?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1996. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying, was there any kind, not only systematic but any kind of violence, the kind that you're talking about, before the terrorists, in an organised manner, started killing civilians, policemen, foresters, post men, Serbs, Albanians and all the other people in Kosovo? Did any violence exist before that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I believe this report "Under Orders" is a good example of the violence that did exist. It was published in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that then later on. But tell me this: Do you know when the indictment was raised, the one that you're testifying about?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Do you mean the initial indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Against me, yes. When was it raised, the indictment?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I believe it was in May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you gave your first statement, as far as I can see here from what I have, the information I have, on the 8th of March already in 1999. That is to say, more than two months prior to the raising of the indictment. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm not clear what you mean by my first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this one here, what I've been provided with.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It says Monday the 8th and Thursday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have two statements, Mr. Abrahams, from you to the Prosecutor, the first dated between the 8th and the 11th of March. That's the one, no doubt, the accused is referring to. The second one, January 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got those in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness should have them. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question at this moment does not refer to the contents of the statement itself, Mr. May, but for the moment just to the date, and the date is Monday the 8th and Thursday the 11th of March, 1999. Before the NATO aggression, two weeks before it, and almost two and a half months before the indictment was raised..

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you give the statement then, during those dates, as it says here?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you do so upon anybody's suggestion?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The investigators, Tim Kelly and Dennis Milner, came to New York City and requested I give a statement, which I agreed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the investigators of this institution came to see you already at the beginning of March 1999 to ask you to give a statement for the indictment against me; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: They asked me to give a statement - it wasn't clear for what purpose that statement was at the time - but about what I had witnessed in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you therefore gave the statement in New York, did you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you say you gave it to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Tim Kelly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was just him that was present when you gave your statement, was it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. There were two investigators who came to New York. Tim Kelly took my statement, and Dennis Milner take the statement of my colleague Peter Bouchkaert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, although this is not, how shall I say, directly connected or a direct question, but it does have significance: Why did you consider that it was necessary to give your statement in keeping with some sort of rules of theirs which passes silently over the names of all sources which you used to make your statement?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: If I understand the correction, you're referring to the redactions in that initial statement which have now been lifted. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. The explanation for that is quite simple, in fact. When I conducted interviews in 1998, there were some individuals who requested anonymity. They asked us not to print their names in our reports, not to make them public. The reason was a fear they had of retaliation, a fear that, in my opinion, was not unfounded or was not unjustified. It was a justified fear. Those interviews -- some of the people requested anonymity. And when I gave this statement to Mr. Kelly, I included some of the names of individuals who had asked us for anonymity. Now, in retrospect, I should have not given him those names, but when I realised they were in there, we asked that those names - I believe there were four names - that those names be redacted in order for us to respect the agreement we had made with the witnesses. The trust between the interviewer and the interviewee is critical. And even though I believe the four individuals would now agree to release their names because the fear is gone, I still had to respect the agreement we made with them in 1998. In the end, we contacted all four individuals and asked them specifically if they minded whether their names be included in my statement, and all four of them agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's all right. We needn't hear any more at greater length. But just tell me, when did you ask them that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That was on Wednesday of this past week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for these three years, you clarified it just last week. Now, you had a scholarship by the Soros Foundation, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I received a -- what's called an individual project fellowship for 18 months, to write my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did you win that fellowship?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Through an application process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign an agreement of any kind, contract, anything like that regarding the fellowship?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I signed a contract once I was awarded the fellowship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the status of a fellowship holder, in view of that contract, does that imply any obligation on your part with respect to your future activities, your job in the future, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The obligation is to use the funds provided by the organisation for the project that -- for the project for which those funds were provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And for which project did you receive those funds?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is to write a book, a journalistic history of Albania's transition from communism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I understand it, you said during the examination-in-chief that you were working on that book at present. It was an ongoing project, the book about Albania's transition from communism.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm still working on the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Soros Foundation is one of the financiers of this particular institution?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: You mean the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the organisation has not funded the Tribunal, but I could be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or George Soros. Was your answer no?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: As far as I know, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me why the government in Tirana extinguished your student newspaper after its first edition?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Our project in Albania was to help the journalism students produce a student newspaper. This paper was published. It was called Reporteri, and four days after its initial publication, the government closed it down, the government of Sali Berisha. I believe it was for a number of reasons which I can explain if -- if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know what the budget is of Human Rights Watch, what budget it had at its disposal in 1998 and 1999? And I'm referring to the area of Kosovo, Macedonia, and Albania, the budget for that.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. The entire budget of Human Rights Watch is published annually in the annual report, and I believe that it is broken down into divisions. For example, the Europe and Central Asia division in which I worked. As for the precise funding for Kosovo and Macedonia, I would have to check with my colleagues, because the research team of which I was a part was separate from the administrative team or specifically the fund-raising team. They brought the money in, we spent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you haven't got an approximation of the budget, perhaps, the budget that was placed at the disposal for the organisation for these purposes, a rough estimate?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I honestly am not prepared to make that estimate because I just don't know. I'm willing to check and that number can be obtained, but I just don't have that figure at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you at least know who finances Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: In general terms, yes. There are essentially three main funding sources: One is donations from wealthy or concerned individuals; another is foundations. I know -- and these are listed in the annual report, but such as the Ford Foundation, the McArthur Foundation, and the Soros Foundation. And a third source is fund-raising activities, like a film festival, an annual dinner, and similar functions. All funding over $5.000 is listed in the annual report, which is public record. And two points I can make briefly about the funding. One is we do not accept any government money. And we also do not accept money from quasi-governmental organisations. By that, I mean an organisation like the National Endowment for Democracy, which is funded by the United States Congress, or the foundations in Germany affiliated with political parties, Friedrich Ebert, Konrad Adenauer Foundation, and so on. Lastly, funding does not have an impact on our findings. It's only one letter but a wide, wide difference between the two. Funders give money but do not have any say in what we find or how we present our research. There is a -- there is a distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, therefore, claim that somebody finances something without any interest in it whatsoever or possibility of influencing that project. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I would distinguish between interest and influencing. Obviously, our supporters - foundations or individuals - are concerned about human rights and believe it's important for Human Rights Watch to conduct its investigations. But these funders do not have an impact on our findings or how we present our findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were, therefore, the first contact person with the representatives of the OTP. That is to say, you had the first contacts with the OTP in New York on the 8th of March, 1999, and it was much later on that you drew up a contact and began working for the OTP. Now, who invited you to work for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely, but certainly I was in touch with Dennis Milner after he visited New York. Yes, I recall that I also was in touch with other individuals who were working in the OTP who expressed to me -- who asked whether I had an interest in contributing -- in working for their office. The concept was that I could assist the OTP based on my knowledge of Kosovo, my knowledge of the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but what I didn't understand was who invited you personally? Who called you up personally from the opposite side? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I mean, officially, I was in touch with the admin, administrative officers who sent me -- I had to fill out a form, I think it's called the P11, if I'm not mistaken, and make a formal application and go through those procedures. But specifically who asked me whether I wanted to do it, I don't recall precisely. I know I was in touch with Clint Williamson, who worked in the OTP, and also with Ivana Nisic, who worked in the OTP, and if my memory is correct, it was mostly with those two people that I was discussing the dates for my work, the possible things that I would work on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in your article published in the Herald Tribune on the 5th of August, as early as the 5th of August, 1998, which is approximately two months before Holbrooke arrived and the Verification Mission was settled in 1998, in August, you wrote the following, and I quote: "The first priority of American policy should be an indictment against Milosevic. For those who are asking themselves whether he can be directly linked up to the crimes in Bosnia and Croatia, a view of the Yugoslav command structure leaves no doubt with respect to his responsibility and accountability for the crimes in Kosovo, which is clearly within the mandate of the Tribunal." Is that one of the sentences you uttered which expresses - how shall I put it? - which anticipates, in fact, a visionary or clairvoyant, if I can use the word, future moves on the part of American policy and politics towards Yugoslavia? And this was in August, published in August 1998.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: First of all, I would have to see the text to verify whether that quote is accurate, but I do believe -- I know that I did say those -- I made -- expressed those general -- that general sentiment. As to whether this eventually happened or not, then we all know that it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have the original here. [In English]: "The first priority for US policy should be the indictment of Milosevic. For those who question whether he could be linked directly to the crimes in Bosnia and Croatia, a look at the Yugoslav chain of command leaves no doubt as to his responsibility for crimes against humanity in Kosovo, which is clearly within the mandate of the international Tribunal for war crimes in the former Yugoslavia." [Interpretation] There's your article, the 5th of August, 1998. You can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's on the bottom of second page.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, this looks accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any further comment you'd like to make about it now, Mr. Abrahams? Has it affected in any way your evidence to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe not, Your Honour. Our call for accountability and our support for this Tribunal as an organisation is consistent with our mandate for justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what are you putting directly to the witness on the basis of the views that he expressed in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, somehow it seems to me -- how shall I put it? It seems to be too much of a visionary thing in relation to the events that ensued much later, because August 1998 is a point in time when it would be difficult for anyone to think of indictments. You know that in October 1998 an agreement was reached on the Verification Mission, and the Verification Mission started in November 1998 and that it ended after Rambouillet, and then the NATO aggression followed. So I am suggesting that this is part of the machinery that worked in preparing the crime against Yugoslavia. Well, that's clear, at least, if it's not clear to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with that. You heard what the suggestion was, Mr. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I adamantly reject the allegation that no one was talking about indictments in August 1998. Human Rights Watch absolutely was talking about indictments, and so were other human rights organisations. As for the visionary nature, the fact that the indictment, arrest, and trial have all occurred should not be attributed to our paragraph. I think the reasons for this process stem from the acts themselves that were committed on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If nothing else, if you are rejecting all of this, isn't this article proof that you and your organisation, Soros, Zimmerman, Abramowitz and all the others were the first who started writing the indictment against me, for reasons that are obvious? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I believe that's not right. Our job is to document violations. We do that. We do not start with an end result, a conclusion or an aim and then search for the facts that will lead us to that conclusion. We start with research in the field that leads us up to the end. The fact that we called for an investigation, the fact that we've called for justice is thoroughly consistent with our raison d'etre, which is to document and monitor and report on abuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But precisely this article, this procedure, doesn't it speak of the contrary, that you started from the end and then you started producing elements that would lead to the desired result that your bosses had in mind? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let him answer. He's a writer, a researcher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given you his answer. He's explained what happened, and he denies this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. All right. All right, Mr. May. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, doesn't it seem to you that this concrete work and activity of yours in relation to this criminal persecution that takes place here, illegally in all fairness but you're taking part in it, doesn't that activity of yours make you unsuitable for testifying here? Especially because you are neither an eyewitness nor an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The accused is alleging bias of some sort on your part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that exactly other than to say that I believe my work at Human Rights Watch was an honest and objective attempt to document the violations that were committed. As for me not being an expert, that I leave to your judgement, but certainly I do consider myself a witness, because as I mentioned in the direct, I had the opportunity to observe some of the crimes firsthand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you see with your very own eyes? Please. Did you see a single killing with your very own eyes?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I witnessed the destruction of civilian property. The burning of Plocica is one example. I witnessed looting. On September 29th near the village of Mlecane, I witnessed policemen carrying boxes and personal goods out of a private home. And I witnessed Gornje Obrinje. I did not witness the killings themselves but I did witness the aftermath; as I mentioned, seven bodies lying in the gully. I also recall that the RTS, the Radio Television Serbia, ran a news piece about the Gornje Obrinje killings which I saw, which claimed that the bodies were actually dolls. Well, I can tell you without any hesitation that I was present in that forest, and I will never in my life forget the smell of the bodies that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that you are objective from every conceivable point of view, and then you brought a photograph of a burned haystack in an Albanian yard, and you did not bring a single photograph of numerous victims of NATO bombings or of massacres committed by the KLA in places such as Klecka or other places that you are aware of. So on the one hand, you bring a picture of a burned haystack, and on the other side, you do not bring a single photograph whatsoever. Is this an illustration of your objectivity?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, it's not true that we have no photographs of KLA crimes or NATO violations. The reports that were presented here today all include photographs of that sort. Perhaps none of them were presented on this machine, and that is a question for the Prosecution. I provided what -- what we thought contributed to this case. But I can certainly go through the reports and show you the photographs that show violations by NATO and the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you will never forget your impressions from Gornje Obrinje. I can understand that. All these scenes have to be horrible. But the question is, do you make a distinction between somebody who is defending himself from terrorism or aggression committed by a foreign power, and this takes place in one's own territory, and on the other hand, somebody who is engaged in terrorism or is carrying out an aggression against an independent state that is resolving its own problems and not jeopardising anybody else? Do you draw a distinction of that kind?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Let me make one thing clear: Human Rights Watch never questioned your government's or any other government's right to confront an armed insurgency within its borders, even through military means. The question is not whether you can confront an insurgency, it's how you confront that insurgency. And our evidence is overwhelming that the forces of the Serbian police and the Yugoslav army did not adequately minimise damage and killing of civilians, and in many cases targeted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you were exploring all of this in 1998, since you had freedom of movement and you communicated with everybody, didn't you know at least then -- there's something wrong with their installations.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that since you were there in 1998 and 1999 until the war --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Somebody's using some machinery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll send a message to stop them. Meanwhile --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, in 1998, you were there. Did you know at least then about the very precise orders that were given, that even the KLA should not be fired at if that could endanger civilians? Could you find that out at least from your own people who were there and who took part in various activities?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that order, no. I have never seen evidence to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you've already mentioned Gornje Obrinje, did I hear you well - and I think I did; by all means it's in the transcript too - that in view of this specific case that you're speaking about, that you explicitly concluded that in that place there had been obvious fighting between the KLA and the police? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. In the fighting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in Gornje Obrinje, if there had been evident fighting between the KLA and the police, on the basis of what can you claim whose fire killed these civilians? Were they killed by KLA fire or police fire or in an unestablished manner? On the basis of what do you ascribe this, in fighting that was evident and that you established to be evident, how do you ascribe this to an intention of the police forces?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The answer to that question is in this book, which I can summarise, of course. There was no question that there was fighting. We believe that 14 Serbian policemen were killed in the fighting that took place in and around Gornje Obrinje. We know that the KLA had a regional base in the town of Likovac, and we know that some villagers of Gornje Obrinje were in the KLA. But we also know that 14 members of the Delijaj family, women and children along with one elderly man whose name I believe was Pajazit, were hiding in the forest. We know this by having inspected the site. There was a small makeshift tent with cooking equipment where they were staying, where they were killed, and by interviewing dozens of people in and around the village. And this comes to the question of our methodology, because our job is to determine how these people were killed, assuming that there is a possibility they were killed -- that they were combatants and killed in combat. We have to assume this might be the case and gather the arguments to prove that it isn't. And in our research, which took place in September and again in December, we concluded that these were civilians hiding in the forest who were attacked, who were murdered. I don't know precisely by whom; special police, PJP, SAJ, MUP reservists, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, we must bring this to a close now because we have to finish and vacate the courtroom. That concludes your answer in any event on that matter. We will resume with cross-examination in the morning. Would you be back at 9.00. Mr. Milosevic, we've determined that you have an extra hour to cross-examine this witness tomorrow. So you should tailor your cross-examination accordingly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean an hour when the entire day has been shortened by one hour when he was examined by Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was examined by Mr. Nice. We have determined the length of that examination. If you have an hour tomorrow, it means that you will have the same time but another 20 minutes or so in addition. So you'll have more than the Prosecution. Now, there was one matter, Mr. Nice, that you wanted to raise. In private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you wouldn't mind waiting just a moment, please, Mr. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of June, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
